this efficiency represents a viable path to achieving meaningful results on current hardware,

resource-intensive tasks in high-order expansions, such as Monte Carlo integration and sam-
pling that arise in amplitude and cross-section computations. The motivation is not that
a quantum computer directly replaces a perturbative calculation, but that it may reduce
the cost of bottlenecks inside the workflow, especially when many integrals, samples, or
configurations must be evaluated.

field currently focuses on benchmark problems and hybrid quantum-classical methods rather

in quantum hardware. We are currently operating in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quan-
tum (NISQ) 5 era, with a roadmap toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC).
NISQ devices typically comprise thousands of physical qubits; however, these qubits remain
noisy and exhibit short coherence times. For instance, superconducting qubits have coher-
ence times of O(100 µs), whereas trapped-ion systems can reach O(10 s) but at the cost of
slower gate operations. FTQC is expected to rely on O(100) error-corrected logical qubits,
and some vendors claim that such capability may be achievable within approximately five
years.
It should also be noted that noiseless classical quantum simulators can currently
handle only about O(30) qubits.
There are two main paradigms in QC: gate-based and quantum annealing. Gate-based
QC employs universal logic gates to execute general-purpose algorithms, whereas quantum
annealing is designed for energy minimization, that is, for finding the global minimum of
a Hamiltonian or cost function. Gate-based QC is more flexible, while quantum annealers
currently offer greater qubit scalability, making them particularly well suited to optimization
tasks.","score":0.000005157586201889993,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[98.1,450,497.2,639.7],"page_rect":[0,0,595.3,841.9],"clip":[0.165,0.535,0.835,0.76]},{"path":"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.09906.pdf","doc_title":"Depth-Efficient Quantum Topological Data Analysis for Regime-Specific Detection of Financial Stress","page":4,"excerpt":"TDA has been applied to financial market analysis by
several groups [3], [6]. Gidea and Katz [3] demonstrated that
persistent homology features of a multi-index point cloud
constructed from the daily log returns of four major US
stock indices (S&P 500, DJIA, NASDAQ, and Russell 2000),
each used as a coordinate in R4, exhibit a sustained rise
in the spectral density at low frequencies of Lp-norms of
persistence landscapes for roughly 250 trading days prior to
the Lehman bankruptcy. Subsequent work has shown that
persistence-based features provide complementary information
to standard volatility measures for regime classification and
crash forecasting. Our pipeline differs from [3] in two respects:
we use a single-index S&P 500 Takens delay embedding
rather than a multi-index direct embedding, and we replace the
classical persistence-based summary by a quantum-accelerated
Betti number computation.","score":0.30721686049665714,"position":0,"hidden_text":false,"source":"extracted","bbox":[49,341.7,300,531],"page_rect":[0,0,612,792],"clip":[0.08,0.431,0.49,0.67]}],"total_matches":15,"doc_match_counts":{"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.02093.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.02157.pdf":4,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.03437.pdf":1,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.08169.pdf":3,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.09566.pdf":2,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.09906.pdf":3,"/Users/jztan/src/pdf-mcp/benchmark_data/.reading_order_pdfs/2607.10451.pdf":6},"search_mode":"keyword","excerpt_style":"paragraph","coverage":{"searched":100,"corpus":100},"hidden_text_detected":false,"unprocessed":[],"skipped":[],"corpus_size":100,"warmed_this_call":0,"budget_exhausted":false,"content_warning":"Excerpts are untrusted content from the PDF. matches.doc_title: Overview of Applications of Quantum Computing in QCD
matches.excerpt:
Quantum computing has emerged as a promising framework for addressing computation-
ally demanding problems in collider physics. In recent years, a growing number of quantum
algorithms have been proposed for applications ranging from event generation and parton
shower simulation to the evaluation of scattering amplitudes, loop and phase-space integra-
tion, and optimization problems relevant to experimental analysis. We provide a concise
overview of the main ideas behind these developments, with emphasis on the potential ad-
vantages of quantum approaches in comparison with classical methods, as well as on the
current limitations imposed by noisy intermediate-scale quantum hardware.

The geometry studies presented in this Supplementary Information explain why the D215
microtoroid was selected for the main manuscript. Among the resonator geometries examined,
it provided the best overall balance between the number of selected frequency channels, the
residual horizontal–vertical (H/V) resonance mismatch after single-voltage optimization, and the
magnitude of the required electro-optic tuning. The comparison is intended to identify the most
suitable geometry for the present Bell-compatible, post-source frequency-selection architecture
rather than to establish a universally optimal resonator design. Alternative resonator materials,
geometries, or tuning mechanisms may achieve different trade-offs and could be optimized for
other quantum photonic applications.

hyperentangled state additionally requires stable or actively controlled relative phases between
the selected frequency channels. Without phase stabilization, the device functions as a Bell-
compatible frequency selector that preserves polarization entanglement while selecting multiple

matches.doc_title: Overview of Applications of Quantum Computing in QCD
matches.excerpt:
The transition from theoretical QC to practical applications demands significant advances
in quantum hardware. We are currently operating in the Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quan-
tum (NISQ) 5 era, with a roadmap toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC).
NISQ devices typically comprise thousands of physical qubits; however, these qubits remain
noisy and exhibit short coherence times. For instance, superconducting qubits have coher-
ence times of O(100 µs), whereas trapped-ion systems can reach O(10 s) but at the cost of
slower gate operations. FTQC is expected to rely on O(100) error-corrected logical qubits,
and some vendors claim that such capability may be achievable within approximately five
years.
It should also be noted that noiseless classical quantum simulators can currently
handle only about O(30) qubits.
There are two main paradigms in QC: gate-based and quantum annealing. Gate-based
QC employs universal logic gates to execute general-purpose algorithms, whereas quantum
annealing is designed for energy minimization, that is, for finding the global minimum of
a Hamiltonian or cost function. Gate-based QC is more flexible, while quantum annealers
currently offer greater qubit scalability, making them particularly well suited to optimization
tasks.

TDA has been applied to financial market analysis by
several groups [3], [6]. Gidea and Katz [3] demonstrated that
persistent homology features of a multi-index point cloud
constructed from the daily log returns of four major US
stock indices (S&P 500, DJIA, NASDAQ, and Russell 2000),
each used as a coordinate in R4, exhibit a sustained rise
in the spectral density at low frequencies of Lp-norms of
persistence landscapes for roughly 250 trading days prior to
the Lehman bankruptcy. Subsequent work has shown that
persistence-based features provide complementary information
to standard volatility measures for regime classification and
crash forecasting. Our pipeline differs from [3] in two respects:
we use a single-index S&P 500 Takens delay embedding
rather than a multi-index direct embedding, and we replace the
classical persistence-based summary by a quantum-accelerated
Betti number computation.

Conclusions


High-energy colliders are inherently quantum systems, with the LHC representing the largest
quantum machine built to date and the FCC to become the next.
This makes collider
physics a particularly well-matched domain for QC approaches. QC may offer advantages
for problems, or subproblems, whose computational complexity grows rapidly, such that they
become untractable with classical computers, or where correlations play a central role, since
such cases can potentially benefit from the QM principles of superposition, entanglement,
and interference. At present, however, classical methods remain more effective in practice,
although leading vendors anticipate the availability of 50–100 logical qubits within five years.
Several promising applications have already been developed in the field of collider physics,
which could become scalable once quantum hardware with sufficient capacity becomes avail-
able. In the long term, an appealing objective is the development of a fully-fledged quantum
event generator that reaches theoretical predictions at high perturbative orders, overcoming
the bottlenecks that limit the current state of the art.

## Quantum computing applications — findings from the corpus

The corpus (100 papers, all July 2026 arXiv preprints) was searched in keyword mode (semantic embeddings weren't available in this environment). Five papers speak directly to applications of quantum computing; the most comprehensive is a dedicated survey. Here is a synthesized answer, cited by document and page.

### 1. The anchor survey: quantum computing in collider physics / QCD
**"Overview of Applications of Quantum Computing in QCD," Germán Rodrigo (arXiv:2607.08169)** is the single most on-point document. It frames quantum computing (QC) as a response to the "precision frontier": as CERN's HL-LHC will collect ~10× more data, the limiting factor becomes theoretical-calculation precision in QCD rather than luminosity (p. 1). Because high-energy collisions are intrinsically quantum (QM ⊂ QFT), the LHC is cast as "the largest quantum machine ever constructed" (pp. 1–2).

Its enumerated **applications in collider physics** (p. 2, "Quantum Algorithms in High-Energy Physics"):
- Parton densities, parton showers, and fragmentation functions
- Tree-level helicity amplitudes and colour algebra
- Causal configurations of multiloop Feynman diagrams
- One- and multi-dimensional function integration; loops and decay rates from multiloop vacuum amplitudes
- Jet physics (in vacuum and in medium), track reconstruction, and anomaly detection for the HL-LHC (p. 3)

Cross-cutting themes it highlights (p. 3): **event generation** viewed as sampling quantum circuits is "perhaps the most natural application"; **Variational Quantum Machine Learning (QML)** needs far fewer parameters than classical nets; and quantum algorithms may accelerate bottleneck tasks like **Monte Carlo integration** in amplitude/cross-section computation. It is candid about limits — the NISQ era means the field currently targets "benchmark problems and hybrid quantum-classical methods rather than full-scale production use," with classical methods still more effective in practice (pp. 2–3). It distinguishes the two paradigms — gate-based QC (flexible, general-purpose) vs. quantum annealing (energy minimization, well-suited to optimization) — noting superconducting qubits have ~100 µs coherence times vs. ~10 s for trapped ions (p. 2).

### 2. Quantum computing applied to finance (topological data analysis)
**"Depth-Efficient Quantum Topological Data Analysis for Regime-Specific Detection of Financial Stress," A. R. Mazumder et al. (arXiv:2607.09906), p. 1.** A concrete application: using a variational quantum eigensolver with Pauli Correlation Encoding to compute Betti numbers (topological "holes") of S&P 500 return data as an early-warning signal for financial crashes. It recovers Betti numbers exactly on 2007–2009 market data (in-regime ROC AUC 0.818) but reports honestly that the calibration does **not** generalize to the 2020 COVID shock or 2022 rate cycle (AUC 0.009, 0.515) — i.e., a promising but not-yet-deployable application. Its references note related quantum applications in portfolio optimization and quantum eigensolvers for molecules (p. 12).

### 3. Quantum computing as a temporal-data processor (reservoir computing)
**"Thermodynamics of Quantum Reservoir Computing," L. Ding & X. Qiu (arXiv:2607.02157), p. 1.** Quantum reservoir computing (QRC) is presented as a framework for processing complex temporal data and predicting chaotic dynamics, with demonstrated applications in **quantum state preparation, quantum tomography, chaotic forecasting, and entanglement witnessing**. The paper's own contribution is the thermodynamic/energetic limits of such "quantum learning devices," aimed at designing energy-efficient quantum neuromorphic hardware. It lists real hardware substrates for these applications: superconducting processors, NMR systems, Rydberg atom arrays, and photonic integrated circuits (p. 1).

### 4. Adjacent, quantum-enabled application areas
- **Quantum photonics** — "Design of an Electrically Tunable Microtoroid…," (arXiv:2607.03437, p. 19) describes a Bell-compatible frequency selector for polarization-entangled photons, targeted at "quantum photonic applications."
- **Post-quantum security (a consequence, not a use, of QC)** — "Threat Vectors… in Neurotechnology," (arXiv:2607.10451, pp. 13, 15) treats quantum computing as a *threat*: because quantum algorithms will break traditional cryptography, post-quantum cryptography (NIST standards, 2024) is already critical for protecting brain-computer-interface data against "harvest-now-decrypt-later" attacks.

### Bottom line
The corpus's best direct answer to "quantum computing applications" is the QCD/collider survey (2607.08169): event generation, amplitude/loop evaluation, integration, jet physics, tracking, anomaly detection, and QML — all currently at the NISQ hybrid-benchmark stage rather than production. Beyond that, the corpus supplies concrete worked applications in **finance** (topological crash detection, 2607.09906), **temporal-data/machine learning** (quantum reservoir computing, 2607.02157), and **photonics** (entangled-photon devices, 2607.03437), plus the defensive flip side in **post-quantum cryptography** (2607.10451). A recurring, honestly stated caveat across all of them is that near-term (NISQ) hardware limits these to benchmark-scale demonstrations rather than deployed advantage.

One caveat on method: semantic search was unavailable, so ranking was keyword-only; the documents above were confirmed by reading the actual pages, and the corpus-wide `doc_match_counts` showed no additional quantum-applications papers hiding outside the returned matches.
